statement: Six children sit round a table. Each child always tells the truth or always lies. Every child says: "The child on my left is a liar." How many liars are at the table?

choices.misconception: I assumed everyone was telling the truth because they all said the same thing.
I checked only what the liars said and used the pattern liar, truth-teller, truth-teller, which gives 2 liars.
I checked only what the truth-tellers said and used the pattern truth-teller, liar, liar, which gives 4 liars.
I thought that if everyone says the same thing, they must all be liars.

hints: What is true about the child to the left of a truth-teller? Of a liar?
Check both kinds of child. A truth-teller's claim must be true, and a liar's claim must be false. Work out what each one says about its left neighbour, then go round the table.
A truth-teller has a liar on its left. A liar's claim is false, so a liar has a truth-teller on its left. So the children must alternate all the way round the table.

solutions.reliable: Take any child. If the child tells the truth, the child on the left really is a liar. If the child lies, the statement is false, so the child on the left tells the truth. So going round the table the children alternate: truth-teller, liar, truth-teller, liar, and so on. With 6 seats this works and gives 3 liars and 3 truth-tellers. Check that all six statements fit: each truth-teller has a liar on the left and each liar has a truth-teller on the left. The transferable idea: test both kinds of speaker and look for the pattern they force.
solutions.elegant: Two liars cannot sit side by side, and nor can two truth-tellers, so the two kinds must alternate. Six seats in a circle split evenly: 3 liars.

whyOnTest: Truth-teller puzzles check whether you test both cases, true and false, instead of trusting the statement; a circle adds a pattern to spot.
